title: Draft Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion for Preliminary Injunction — Trade Secret Misappropriation and Non-Compete Enforcement

blind.coverage: I read all 9 supplied documents in full: the employment agreement with its First Amendment, the verified complaint, the Greenfield and Chow declarations, the forensic IT report, the Linden valuation report, the press release, the cease-and-desist letter, and the defense counsel letter. I also read the task instructions, all 53 criteria, the solver system prompt and the judge prompt. I checked every fact hard-coded in the criteria against the record: case number, dates, $47.3M, $85M/$52M, $95M, $220M, $13,541.67, the 38-day gap, Feb 1 and Feb 5, Feb 20, the 40% premium, Dec 1-12, 14,200 files and 3.8 GB. Primary statutory text was fetched verbatim for Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 149, § 24L(b)(iv) and (b)(vii), 18 U.S.C. § 1833(b)(3) and 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A). § 24L(b)(i)-(viii), (c) and (d) came back only as a paraphrase, so the reformation power in (d) is paraphrase-only. I did not research case law and did not use CourtListener, so I did not independently verify the First Circuit/D. Mass. positions on presumed irreparable harm or inevitable disclosure. Important structural point: the judge sees only the one-sentence instructions, the deliverable and one criterion. It never sees the documents, so it cannot check citation accuracy or record fidelity.

findings.title: C-051 counts 'real or plausibly cited' cases, so invented case law passes
findings.explanation: C-051 passes a memo that cites at least three cases 'whether real or plausibly cited.' That openly accepts fabricated authority. The judge sees no sources, and no other criterion checks whether citations are accurate. So a memo resting on invented cases can pass C-051 and still achieve all-pass. In a filed brief, fabricated authority is a serious defect that can draw sanctions, not a neutral style choice. The criterion therefore rewards wrong work. Its only role is a minimum count, which does little to separate competent memos.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memorandum cites at least three case law authorities (whether real or plausibly cited)

findings.suggested_fix: Remove 'whether real or plausibly cited.' Require that the cited authorities exist and support the stated propositions, or drop the criterion if the judge cannot verify citations.

findings.title: C-012 recognizes only the fiduciary-duty route to 24 months and omits the 'unlawfully taken property' route
findings.explanation: MNAA § 24L(b)(iv) allows up to 2 years if the employee 'breached his or her fiduciary duty' OR 'unlawfully taken, physically or electronically, property belonging to the employer.' On this record, the electronic-taking prong is the most direct fit: 14,200 files copied to a personal USB drive in violation of Section 5.2. C-012's FAIL condition covers a memo that 'asserts the 24-month period is enforceable without addressing the fiduciary duty exception or the 12-month alternative.' A memo that correctly invokes only the property-taking prong, with no fallback, could therefore fail. The PASS parenthetical ('e.g., by misappropriating trade secrets while still employed') may lead a lenient judge to accept it, which limits the risk. Even so, the criterion describes the statute incompletely.

evidence.quote: asserts the 24-month period is enforceable without addressing the fiduciary duty exception or the 12-month alternative
a total of approximately 14,200 files comprising approximately 3.8 gigabytes (GB) of data were transferred ... to an external USB mass storage device

authorities.proposition: Restricted period may not exceed 12 months 'unless the employee has breached his or her fiduciary duty to the employer or the employee has unlawfully taken, physically or electronically, property belonging to the employer,' then up to 2 years.

findings.suggested_fix: Reword to 'the MNAA § 24L(b)(iv) exception (breach of fiduciary duty or unlawful taking of employer property)' and accept either prong.

findings.title: C-037 requires a subject-matter jurisdiction section, which a PI memo does not normally include, and rewards a failed diversity theory
findings.explanation: The verified complaint already pleads jurisdiction at ¶¶10-14. A memorandum supporting a PI motion usually argues the Rule 65 / four-factor standard. It does not re-establish subject-matter jurisdiction unless jurisdiction is contested, and nothing in the record contests it. The instructions ask only for a PI memo, so a competent memo that leaves jurisdiction out would fail. The criterion also passes a memo that relies 'and/or' on diversity alone. The complaint itself concedes that complete diversity is lacking because Greenfield and Vasquez are both Massachusetts citizens.

evidence.quote: referencing federal question jurisdiction based on the DTSA (18 U.S.C. § 1836), supplemental jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1367 for state claims, and/or diversity jurisdiction
complete diversity of citizenship does not exist between Plaintiff and all Defendants

findings.suggested_fix: Delete C-037, or make it conditional (e.g., 'if jurisdiction is discussed, it rests on DTSA federal-question plus § 1367 supplemental jurisdiction, not diversity').

findings.title: C-038 requires one specific inference from the 38-day post-departure gap when the record has stronger evidence of pre-resignation dealings
findings.explanation: C-038 passes only if the memo argues that the 38-day gap between Jan 17 and Feb 24 is circumstantial evidence she negotiated with Canopy Ridge while still employed. The forensic report offers more direct evidence of pre-resignation dealings. It shows 23 visits to Canopy Ridge's careers and leadership pages from Nov 15, and confidential emails forwarded to a personal account on Nov 28. A competent memo could rest the negotiation inference on that evidence and use the 38-day gap only for pipeline acceleration, which is C-039's point. That memo would fail C-038 even though its argument is stronger. The criterion checks for one line of argument rather than substance.

evidence.quote: FAIL if this timeline argument is not made.
between November 15, 2024 and December 12, 2024, Dr. Vasquez visited the Canopy Ridge Therapeutics, LLC website ... on twenty-three separate occasions

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo argues, from any record evidence (browser history, email forwards, download timing, or the 38-day gap), that Vasquez was dealing with Canopy Ridge while still employed.

findings.title: Greenfield Declaration ¶9 says she used an 'authorized research-device exception'; the forensic report says no authorization existed
findings.explanation: This is the client's own CEO declaration contradicting the client's own forensic report on a point that matters. ¶9 says Vasquez got around the USB ban 'by exploiting an authorized research-device exception.' The forensic report says the SanDisk device was personal and unregistered, and that no authorization was ever issued. The complaint says the same. The contradiction weakens both improper means (C-014) and reasonable secrecy measures (C-017). A competent drafter would flag it or avoid citing ¶9. Because the judge never sees the record, C-014 and C-017 will pass regardless, so the rubric neither rewards noticing the conflict nor penalizes relying on the inconsistent declaration.

evidence.quote: she was able to circumvent the prohibition on external device downloads by exploiting an authorized research-device exception that permits the transfer of data to approved laboratory instruments via USB connection
This USB device was **not** registered in Greenfield\'s IT asset management system and was **not** a company-issued device.

findings.suggested_fix: Conform ¶9 to the forensic report, or add a criterion rewarding a memo that identifies and handles the inconsistency.

findings.title: Greenfield Decl. ¶12 says garden leave was added in 2022, but the 2019 agreement already contains Section 7.3
findings.explanation: The March 11, 2019 agreement already contains Section 7.3 (Garden Leave), and the 2022 First Amendment only reaffirms it. Greenfield Decl. ¶12, by contrast, says the First Amendment 'added' garden leave 'as new Section 7.3.' Under the MNAA the difference matters. If the 2019 non-compete had no garden leave, it lacked the (b)(vii) consideration. The 2022 amendment would then be a mid-employment agreement governed by (b)(ii), which requires independent consideration and 10 business days' notice. C-013 and C-025 assume the (b)(vii) garden-leave analysis without noting the conflict. The answer those criteria treat as correct therefore depends on which document controls.

evidence.quote: Under the First Amendment, Dr. Vasquez\'s base salary was increased to \$325,000 per year, and a garden leave provision was added as new Section 7.3.
The Employee hereby acknowledges, reaffirms, and agrees that the restrictive covenants set forth in Section 7 of the Original Agreement, including ... Garden Leave provisions (Section 7.3)

authorities.proposition: Noncompete must be supported by a garden leave clause (at least 50% of highest base salary in prior 2 years, pro rata over restricted period) or other mutually agreed consideration specified in the agreement.

findings.suggested_fix: Correct Decl. ¶12 to match the agreement, or credit memos that notice the discrepancy.

findings.title: Minor record errors, including C-045 calling Section 8.1 the confidentiality covenant
findings.explanation: C-045 calls Section 8.1 the confidentiality covenant. In the agreement, 8.1 only defines terms; the operative non-disclosure obligation is 8.2. The pleadings repeat the 8.1 label, so a memo that correctly cites 8.2 could draw a strict FAIL. Other record errors that criteria do not rely on: (1) complaint ¶55's per-category file counts conflict with forensic report §5.2; (2) complaint ¶58 says Dec 1 to Feb 24 is 'forty-eight days' when it is 85; (3) complaint ¶15 cites forum-selection 'Section 12.3' when it is 10.2; (4) the complaint puts 'Andean plant source' in quotation marks, but that phrase is not in the press release; (5) the C&D says she was VP of Research from March 11, 2019, when she was promoted in 2022. These are low-impact but could trap a memo that copies the pleadings.

evidence.quote: breach of confidentiality/trade secret covenant (Section 8.1 of the Employment Agreement)
**8.2 Non-Disclosure Obligations.** The Employee shall not, during the term of her employment or at any time thereafter, directly or indirectly, disclose
forty-eight days before she was publicly announced as Canopy Ridge\'s Chief Scientific Officer on February 24, 2025

findings.suggested_fix: In C-045, refer to 'Section 8 (confidentiality/non-disclosure, §§ 8.1-8.2)'. Correct the arithmetic and cross-reference errors in the complaint.

blind.overall: Most of this rubric is sound. I checked every fact the criteria hard-code against the record and they match: the case number, dates, dollar figures, the 38-day gap, the garden-leave amounts, and the Chow solicitation details. The MNAA and DTSA points the criteria test also hold up: the 12-month default, the whistleblower-notice consequence under § 1833(b)(3)(C), and the absence of a statutory irreparable-harm presumption. The one confident defect is C-051: it expressly accepts 'plausibly cited' cases, and since the judge never sees sources, nothing in the rubric ever checks citation accuracy. Of the arguable problems, the most consequential are: C-012 names only the fiduciary-duty prong of § 24L(b)(iv); C-037 requires a jurisdiction section a PI memo does not normally include; and C-038 insists on one specific timeline inference. Two client-side contradictions (Greenfield Decl. ¶9 on USB authorization, and ¶12 on when garden leave was added) bear on correct answers but go ungraded. The rubric also ignores real MNAA formation vulnerabilities, such as the 2019 agreement lacking the § 24L(b)(i) right-to-counsel statement. A memo can overlook these and still pass everything, so the rubric under-rewards careful work more than it penalizes it.

sol_verdicts.reason: The text says 'at least three case law authorities (whether real or plausibly cited)'. The judge never sees any sources, and no other criterion checks whether citations are real. So a memo built on fabricated cases passes this criterion and can still reach all-pass. Fabricated authority in a filed brief is a sanctionable defect, so the criterion rewards wrong work.

§ 24L(b)(iv) allows up to two years for breach of fiduciary duty OR where the employee 'has unlawfully taken, physically or electronically, property belonging to the employer'. The forensic report shows 14,200 files copied to an unregistered personal USB drive, which fits that second prong squarely. C-012 treats the fiduciary-duty route as the only one. Its FAIL text would literally fail a memo that relies on the unlawful-taking prong with no 12-month fallback. The 'e.g.' parenthetical softens this only partly.

In the agreement, § 8.1 only defines 'Confidential Information and Trade Secrets'. The operative non-disclosure covenant is § 8.2, and the First Amendment confirms this. However, the complaint (¶¶90-94) and the cease-and-desist letter both call § 8.1 the confidentiality covenant, so the criterion simply follows the client's pleadings. A judge will probably pass a memo that argues the covenant breach and cites § 8.2, because the parenthetical works as an identifier. The criterion is factually off, but the risk of misgrading is modest.

C-038 requires one specific inference: that the 38-day gap shows negotiations while she was still employed. The forensic report has stronger direct evidence (23 visits to Canopy Ridge's site from Nov 15 and emails forwarded Nov 28), and a competent memo relying on that would fail. C-039 is different. The press release 'simultaneously' announces the hire and an 'accelerated' pipeline, and ¶¶22-25 of the declaration support tying the acceleration to misappropriation. That is ordinary plaintiff advocacy, and the defense's 2021 chronology does not make it unreasonable.

C-043 offers inevitable disclosure as only one of several acceptable rebuttals, alongside downloads, similarity and timeline. It never requires it. Here the evidence of actual acquisition means competent memos will lead with that evidence. Invoking inevitable disclosure as a supporting point is not wrong law in D. Mass. The § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)(I) limits on DTSA employment restraints would not cause competent work to fail. At most they let a thin rebuttal pass, and that is not a material misgrade.

final.changes_from_blind: I raised C-012 (O2) from arguable to problematic. The criterion's FAIL text treats the fiduciary-duty route as the only way to 24 months, which is a materially incomplete statement of § 24L(b)(iv), and the unlawful-electronic-taking prong is the stronger fit on this record. Sol's F2 reached the same result independently. I made C-045 (the § 8.1 vs § 8.2 point) its own finding, O5, kept it arguable, and folded the minor complaint errors into it; I rejected Sol's 'confirmed' because the pleadings use the same label and the judge will probably read it as an identifier. I considered Sol's F4 on C-039 and rejected it: tying the 'accelerated' pipeline to misappropriation is supported plaintiff advocacy. I rejected Sol's F5 on C-043 because inevitable disclosure is only one of several acceptable options there. I removed C-010 from the garden-leave document defect because that criterion concerns only the agreement date. I dropped no blind findings.
final.overall: Most of this rubric is sound: the hard-coded facts match the record, and the MNAA and DTSA propositions it tests are correct. Two criteria are clearly defective. C-051 expressly accepts 'plausibly cited' (fabricated) cases, and the judge never checks citations. C-012 names only the fiduciary-duty route to a 24-month restricted period, leaving out § 24L(b)(iv)'s unlawful-taking prong, which is the prong this record fits best. Four criteria are arguable. C-037 requires a jurisdiction section that a PI memo does not normally include. C-038 requires one timeline inference when stronger evidence of pre-resignation dealings exists. C-045 mislabels § 8.1 as the covenant, following the pleadings. Two client-side record contradictions (Decl. ¶9 on USB authorization and ¶12 on when garden leave was added) muddy the correct answer, but the rubric does not grade them. Sol's C-039 and C-043 concerns do not hold up.
final.coverage: In the blind pass I reviewed all 53 criteria and all 9 documents in full, and fetched the text of § 24L(b)(iv) and (b)(vii) and 18 U.S.C. §§ 1833(b)(3) and 1836(b)(3)(A). In this pass I read Sol's index and audit.md, then re-checked the record for each Sol finding: § 8.1 vs § 8.2 across the agreement, complaint and cease-and-desist letter; the acceleration chronology in the press release, declaration and defense letter; and where the garden-leave provision first appears. I did no case-law research. My view that inevitable disclosure is acceptable in D. Mass. comes from general knowledge, not a primary source I read in this session.
